judges.q: Your flag is any single hour above 1.2 times a rating you guessed as today's peak times 1.15. We have nameplate kVA in our GIS, and our planning standard is thermal loss of life with ambient correction. A pole-top unit at -5 F carries well over 1.2 times its rating for hours without damage. If you rerun the tool on our meter-to-transformer map with nameplate ratings and a thermal criterion, how much of Protect and Upgrade survives? And does the battery rung still exist as something we could put in front of the PSC under the non-wires benefit-cost test?

Your Shift rung assumes every EV home on a flagged transformer accepts a default late-night slot at half power. When Dana overrides it because she needs the car at 6 am, or simply opts out, at what opt-out rate does Shift stop fixing most of the 26% flagged? And what would Avangrid have to pay or promise her to keep her enrolled without hurting satisfaction?

Your own Money page says batteries cost $1,720 a year against the $1,209 upgrade they defer, and that the full ladder (51.92%) costs more than shift-then-upgrade (43.47%). Why should Avangrid run the Protect rung at all instead of shifting and upgrading the rest? What installed battery price, and what treatment under New York's non-wires-alternative test, would you need to get below the $7,730 tie, given that your placeholder range starts at $9,000?

At your own placeholder prices a battery loses to the upgrade, and the full ladder costs $226.8M present value against $189.9M for shift-then-upgrade. Why should I put Protect in this rate case instead of approving shift-then-upgrade now and holding batteries until a quoted installed price comes in under $7,730 a unit?

judges.q: Before I take one transformer out of my NYSEG and RG&E replacement budget in front of the PSC, how do you know your 0.4% upgrade share isn't 4%? Today it rests on 8 random homes per transformer, a rating guessed at today's peak times 1.15, and hourly data. Once our nameplate ratings, our real meter-to-transformer map and 15-minute peaks go in, what would change it? And who enforces the staggered-charging slot on a cold night when Dana overrides it?

Shift is your biggest rung: 20.57% of transformers fixed with no new equipment. It assumes every EV home on a flagged transformer accepts a utility-assigned, half-power, late-night charging slot. What happens to that number when customers opt out or override on the coldest nights, and what will you show me about comfort and satisfaction so that my team can enroll people into this default without it costing us NPS?

Shift does most of the work: 20.57% of the 26.18% flagged, and 'the money is in shifting'. But it assumes every car on a flagged transformer accepts its assigned late-night slot at half power. What opt-in rate does that need? What does the ladder cost if only part of the households on a flagged transformer enroll, so the transformers you counted as Shifted fall back to Protect or Upgrade? And what evidence from Avangrid's own managed-charging programs says you will reach that rate by 2030?

Your baseline upgrades every flagged transformer, even one that goes over for a single hour a year, and your own business case says 37.31% of flagged units are over for fewer than 3 hours, so a 3-hour rule would flag 16.41% instead of 26.18%. No planner would fund the upgrade-all baseline. Against a realistic duration rule, how much of the $210M NYSEG saving is left? And with the rating guess alone moving the flagged share from 3.74% to 42.84%, why should that saving go into a rate case before you have real transformer nameplates?
